title: The history of the sprinkler
tagline: 2,000 years from a steam toy that spun in Alexandria to circles of green you can see from an aeroplane.
intro: A sprinkler does a simple thing: it breaks a stream of water into drops and spreads them evenly. The idea of a jet that turns its own nozzle is ancient, but a sprinkler needs water under pressure in a pipe, and that only reached homes and farms in the 1800s. From then on two families grew side by side: sprinklers that water lawns and crops, and sprinklers that wait in the ceiling for a fire. This is the story of both, from Alexandria to California to the fields of India.

eras.name: A jet that turns itself
eras.summary: Hero's steam ball and Segner's water wheel show that a jet pushes back on its nozzle. Nobody yet has piped water to use the idea.

eras.name: Water in a pipe
eras.summary: Cities lay water mains. Inventors drill holes in pipes to fight fires, patent the first lawn sprinklers, and make a fire sprinkler that opens by itself.

eras.name: The steady beat
eras.summary: A citrus grower's impact sprinkler, a way to measure evenness, and a pipe on wheels that walks round a field turn the sprinkler into a farm machine.

eras.name: Every drop counted
eras.summary: Drip irrigation arrives as a rival. Rain guns, gear drives and low-pressure pivots follow, and fire sprinklers learn to act faster.

eras.name: Per drop, more crop
eras.summary: India puts public money behind sprinklers and drippers on millions of small farms, and physicists settle an old sprinkler puzzle.

events.title: A ball that spins on its own steam
events.text: Hero described the aeolipile: a hollow ball on a pivot, with two bent nozzles pointing opposite ways. Steam from a boiling pot below rushed out of the nozzles and the ball spun round. The Roman writer Vitruvius had mentioned a device of the same name about a century earlier, so Hero may not have been first.
events.why: It is the first recorded reaction engine. A jet goes one way, the nozzle is pushed the other way: the same push turns a spinning lawn sprinkler.

events.title: Segner's water wheel
events.text: Segner, a professor born in what is now Bratislava, built a wheel driven by water in place of steam. Water ran down into an upright cylinder and left through bent arms at the bottom. The jets pushed the arms backwards and the wheel turned.
events.why: Swap Hero's steam for water and you have the spinning-arm sprinkler. The Segner wheel was also an ancestor of the water turbine.

events.title: A theatre with holes in its pipes
events.where: Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, London, England
events.text: After the old theatre burned down, Colonel William Congreve patented a way to protect the new one. Pipes pierced with rows of small holes ran through the building, fed from a large airtight tank. If a fire broke out, someone opened a valve outside and water rained from the pipes. Accounts say the system was fitted when the theatre was rebuilt in 1812.
events.why: It is widely described as the first sprinkler system in a building. But it was not automatic: a person had to notice the fire and turn the valve.

events.title: A patent for watering the lawn
events.text: Joseph Lessler received US patent 121,949 for an 'improvement in lawn-sprinklers'. It was a stand with a swivelling nozzle, joined to the hydrant by a hose that could be coiled in a basket. He wrote that it would sprinkle lawns and gardens without the constant attention of an attendant.
events.why: It is often called the first American lawn sprinkler patent. Patents for garden and hose sprinklers with lower numbers were granted earlier the same year, so 1871 is best seen as the year the idea arrived. Piped water under pressure was reaching more and more houses, and a sprinkler is no use without it.

events.title: A sprinkler that opens by itself
events.text: Parmelee ran the Mathushek piano factory, full of dry wood and varnish, and wanted cheaper fire insurance. He patented a sprinkler head held shut by a cap soldered in place. In a fire the solder melted, the cap fell away and water sprayed out. Philip W. Pratt of Abington, Massachusetts, had patented an automatic sprinkler in 1872, which is why some call Parmelee's the second.
events.why: Parmelee's was the first automatic sprinkler head to be made and fitted in numbers. Heat alone opens it, and only above the fire.

events.title: Grinnell makes it dependable
events.text: Grinnell's pipe company made Parmelee's sprinklers under licence. He then designed a better one, more sensitive to heat and tighter against leaks, and patented it in 1881. In 1890 he brought out the glass disc sprinkler. He took out about 40 patents on sprinklers in all.
events.why: Grinnell turned a clever idea into a product that factory owners and insurers trusted. A sprinkler has to stay shut for years and still open at once.

events.title: Mach's puzzle: what if it sucks?
events.text: In his book The Science of Mechanics, the physicist Ernst Mach described a little reaction wheel that spins when air is blown out of it. Then he asked what happens when air is sucked in. He reported that it showed no distinct rotation.
events.why: It is the first written form of the 'reverse sprinkler' question. Physicists argued about it for the next 140 years.

events.title: Rain from a pipe on posts
events.text: Charles Skinner, a grower in Ohio, set long pipes on wooden posts above his crops, with a small nozzle every three feet or so. Turning the pipe on its supports swept the row of jets from side to side. Trade histories date his patent to 1894. His Skinner Irrigation Company sold the 'Skinner System' to market gardens, nurseries and golf courses for decades.
events.why: It was one of the first sprinkler systems for crops, and it brought overhead watering from the lawn to the field.

events.title: One rule book for sprinklers
events.who: Insurers and a pipe maker, later the National Fire Protection Association
events.text: In 1895 there were nine different sets of rules for sprinkler pipes within 100 miles of Boston. Fitters could not keep up. A group of insurance men and a pipe maker met to agree on one standard. They published it in 1896 and founded the National Fire Protection Association that November.
events.why: Those rules grew into NFPA 13, the standard still used to design fire sprinkler systems around the world.

events.title: A glass bulb that bursts
events.who: Engineers of the Grinnell company, with advice from Thomas Edison
events.text: Grinnell's engineers replaced the solder link with a small sealed bulb of quartz glass filled with liquid. Heat makes the liquid swell until the bulb shatters and lets the water out. On 20 April 1921 a Grinnell man visited Thomas Edison's laboratory to ask which liquid to use. The Science Museum in London holds a Grinnell 'quartzoid' bulb sprinkler dated 1927.
events.why: The coloured glass bulb is now the most familiar part of a fire sprinkler. It does not corrode, and the liquid sets the temperature at which it opens.

events.title: The sprinkler that goes tick, tick, tick
events.text: Englehart grew citrus and wanted a sprinkler that turned slowly and threw water far. In 1933 he built one with a spring-loaded arm. The jet knocks the arm aside, the spring swings it back, and it strikes the sprinkler body and nudges it round a little. He applied for a patent on 18 December 1933 and it was granted as US 1,997,901 on 16 April 1935. The patent spells his name Englehart. The landmark plaque spells it Englehardt.
events.why: A slow turn gives the jet time to reach its full distance. The impact sprinkler watered large areas evenly with one moving part, and it spread across the world's farms.

events.title: Made in the family barn
events.text: Englehart preferred farming to business. His friend Clement LaFetra had urged him to patent the sprinkler, and Englehart assigned all the rights to Clement and his wife Mary Elizabeth. Production began in the LaFetra family barn on 13 October 1935. They named the company Rain Bird.
events.why: A husband and wife turned a neighbour's invention into the best known name in sprinklers.

events.title: Feynman floods the cyclotron lab
events.text: As a student, Richard Feynman argued with friends about Mach's puzzle. He tested it in the cyclotron laboratory with a tiny sprinkler inside a big glass bottle, using air pressure to push water backwards through it. Edward Creutz, who was there, recalled a small tremor and then no movement. Feynman turned up the pressure and the bottle exploded. He told the story in his 1985 book 'Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!' and did not give the answer.
events.why: The puzzle got his name, and thousands of physics students have argued about it since.

events.title: A number for evenness
events.text: Christiansen, an irrigation engineer, set out rows of cans under sprinklers and measured the water each one caught. In Bulletin 670, 'Irrigation by Sprinkling', he turned the readings into one number: the uniformity coefficient. It is 100 per cent when every can catches the same amount, and it falls as the cans differ more from the average.
events.why: For the first time, growers and makers could compare sprinklers and spacings with a number. Christiansen's coefficient is still used to design sprinkler systems.

events.title: A pipe that walks in a circle
events.text: Zybach, a tenant farmer and tinkerer, built a long pipe carried on wheeled towers that crept round a central well, sprinkling as it went. The water pressure itself drove the towers. He applied for a patent on 27 June 1949 and received US 2,604,359 on 22 July 1952. Accounts differ on when he first built it: some say 1940, others 1947 or 1948.
events.why: The centre pivot waters a whole field with no one moving pipes. It is the reason farmland looks like rows of green circles from an aeroplane.

events.title: Valley takes the pivot to market
events.text: Zybach and his partner A. E. Trowbridge made pivots in Columbus, Nebraska, and sold only 19 in two years. In 1954 they sold the manufacturing rights to Robert Daugherty's small firm, Valley Manufacturing. Its engineers spent the next ten years making the machine taller, stronger and more reliable. The firm became Valmont Industries.
events.why: By 1992 more than 110,000 centre pivots were watering about 14 million acres in the United States alone.

events.title: Betty LaFetra takes Rain Bird worldwide
events.text: Clement LaFetra died in 1963. Mary Elizabeth LaFetra, who had owned the sprinkler rights with him since the start, became the company's second chief executive and led it until 1978. Under her the company began selling around the world.
events.why: A woman ran one of the largest irrigation companies in the world for 15 years, at a time when very few women led engineering firms.

events.title: Drip: the sprinkler's quiet rival
events.who: Simcha Blass, Yeshayahu Blass and Kibbutz Hatzerim
events.text: In the 1930s a farmer showed the water engineer Simcha Blass a big tree that grew 'without water'. A leaking pipe joint was feeding its roots drop by drop. Years later, with cheap plastic pipe to hand, Blass and his son designed a dripper that lets water out slowly through a long narrow channel. On 10 August 1965 they signed a contract with Kibbutz Hatzerim to found Netafim. Production began in 1966.
events.why: Drip puts water at the roots, not in the air. Sprinkler and drip together are now called micro-irrigation, and they compete for the same fields.

events.title: The rain gun
events.text: The Nelson family had made hose fittings and sprinklers in Peoria, Illinois, since 1911. In 1972 they started a new company in Walla Walla. Its first products included the Big Gun: a very large sprinkler that throws one heavy jet tens of metres.
events.why: One rain gun can do the work of dozens of small sprinklers. India's micro-irrigation scheme lists rain guns that throw 24 to 36 metres, for watering large areas in a short time.

events.title: Fire sprinklers come home
events.who: National Fire Protection Association and Grinnell
events.text: For a century, fire sprinklers protected mills, warehouses and shops, not houses. In May 1975 the NFPA adopted a standard for sprinklers in one- and two-family homes, called NFPA 13D. In 1981 Grinnell received the first listing for a residential sprinkler, built to open faster in a small room.
events.why: Most fire deaths happen at home. A quick-opening sprinkler is meant to keep a room survivable until people get out.

events.title: Dropping the water low
events.text: Fuel prices had soared and the Ogallala aquifer was sinking. At a research station on the Texas High Plains, Lyle and Bordovsky hung tubes down from a moving pivot so that water was placed gently between the crop rows at low pressure. They began in 1978 and published the method, called LEPA, in 1981.
events.why: Spray thrown high into hot wind partly evaporates. Putting the water low saves water and pumping energy.

events.title: Gears take over the lawn
events.text: Edwin Hunter had sold gear-driven sprinklers since about 1960 through an earlier firm, Moist O'Matic, which he sold to Toro in 1962. In 1981 he and his son Paul founded Hunter Industries to make the PGP, a small pop-up sprinkler turned by a water-driven turbine and a train of gears. The company dates its launch to 1983.
events.why: A gear drive is quiet and sealed against grit. On lawns and sports fields it largely replaced the ticking impact sprinkler.

events.title: Micro-irrigation made in Jalgaon
events.text: Bhavarlal Jain had sold tractors, pipes and sprinkler sets to farmers in Maharashtra since the 1960s, and began making PVC pipe in 1980. In 1987–88 he set up a company to make and promote drip irrigation in India. Jain Irrigation grew into one of the largest micro-irrigation companies in the world.
events.why: Drip lines and sprinklers made in India, at Indian prices, put them within reach of small farmers.

events.title: Sprinklers that beat a warehouse fire
events.text: Tall racks of boxed goods burn too fiercely for ordinary sprinklers, which only hold a fire back. In the 1980s the insurer's laboratory Factory Mutual, working with sprinkler makers, developed the ESFR sprinkler: early suppression, fast response. It opens quickly and drops large, heavy drops that punch down through the flames. The test standard for it, UL 1767, was first published in 1990.
events.why: It was a new aim for a fire sprinkler: to put the fire out, not just to control it.

events.title: India backs drip and sprinkler
events.who: Department of Agriculture and Cooperation, Government of India
events.text: A national Task Force on Micro Irrigation, chaired by the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, reported in January 2004 that about 69.5 million hectares of India could use drip or sprinklers. In January 2006 the central government launched a scheme to share the cost of these systems with farmers.
events.why: A sprinkler set costs money before it saves any water. A subsidy lets a small farmer make the switch.

events.title: A national mission
events.text: The 2006 scheme was scaled up into the National Mission on Micro Irrigation, which ran until 2013–14. In 2014–15 it became part of a wider mission on sustainable farming, under the name On Farm Water Management.
events.why: The names kept changing but the idea stayed: help farmers swap flooded furrows for drippers and sprinklers.

events.title: Per Drop More Crop
events.text: The Cabinet approved the Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana on 1 July 2015, with a planned Rs 50,000 crore over five years. Its mottoes were 'Har Khet Ko Pani', water for every field, and 'Per Drop More Crop'. The Per Drop More Crop part pays 55 per cent of the cost of a drip or sprinkler system for small and marginal farmers and 45 per cent for others, for up to five hectares each.
events.why: It made the sprinkler and the dripper a national policy in a country where farming uses most of the water.

events.title: A fund for the states
events.text: The Cabinet approved a Micro Irrigation Fund of Rs 5,000 crore, held by the farm bank NABARD: Rs 2,000 crore for 2018–19 and Rs 3,000 crore for 2019–20. States can borrow from it at a reduced rate of interest to add to the subsidy or to build shared systems.
events.why: By January 2018 about 9.68 million hectares in India were under micro-irrigation from all sources. The fund was meant to speed that up.

events.title: The reverse sprinkler is solved
events.who: Kaizhe Wang, Brennan Sprinkle, Mingxuan Zuo and Leif Ristroph
events.text: A team at New York University floated an S-shaped sprinkler on a bearing with almost no friction and made it suck water in. It turned steadily, in the opposite direction to a normal sprinkler and about 50 times more slowly. The cause was inside: the two streams entering the arms meet in the middle, but not exactly head on, and that gives a small twist. One of the authors really is named Sprinkle.
events.why: It answered the question Mach asked in 1883 and Feynman made famous, with an experiment and with mathematics that agree.

events.title: 115 lakh hectares
events.text: By July 2026, Per Drop More Crop had brought 115 lakh hectares (11.5 million hectares) under drip and sprinkler since 2015–16, about 8 per cent of the land India sows. Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh have added the most. A count in March 2025 showed sprinklers slightly ahead of drip: 50.60 lakh hectares against 46.37.
events.why: In eleven years the area added was larger than the whole of Portugal.

facts: The first Rain Bird sprinklers were made in a family barn in Glendora, California. Production began on 13 October 1935.
A sprinkler that sucks water in does spin, but backwards and about 50 times more slowly. It took until 2024 to show it.
In 1895 there were nine different sets of rules for fire sprinkler pipes within 100 miles of Boston. Sorting that out created the NFPA.
Frank Zybach's first centre pivots were driven by the same water they sprinkled, with no engine and no electricity.
Under India's Per Drop More Crop scheme, sprinklers covered slightly more land than drip by March 2025: 50.60 lakh hectares against 46.37.
